title: Slow to anger (Avot 5:11)
hookLine: hard to anger and easy to calm is the pious temperament
tomorrow: is it bragging to ask other people to give too?

cards: Every friend group has both kinds. One blows up in a second and is laughing two minutes later. One takes forever to get angry, then stays there for a week.
Which is better, the short fuse or the fast cool-down? People argue about it at dinner tables, in break rooms, after a bad game. Avot sorts tempers four ways, and its answer is: neither, on its own.

teach.b: The question: is anger itself the problem? Avot 5:11 doesn't say never be angry. It measures two speeds: how fast anger comes, and how fast it goes.
Easy to anger, easy to calm: the gain is canceled by the loss. Hard to anger, hard to calm: the loss is canceled by the gain. Easy to anger, hard to calm: wicked.
And hard to anger, easy to calm: a chasid, a person of devotion. So the answer is both halves at once.

teach.h: THE CHASID: SLOW IN, QUICK OUT.
teach.b: Slow on the way in, quick on the way out. Here's the thread to a neighbor.

teach.h: JAMES: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO WRATH.
teach.b: Christians read a line close to this in the Letter of James, in the King James Bible: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." The next verse says human anger doesn't work God's righteousness.
Both traditions read Exodus, where God is called long-suffering, slow to anger.
That much is real common ground. And an honest difference. Avot grades a temperament, with mixed cases that cancel out, and asks about the cool-down as much as the fuse.
James ties slowness to anger to listening first: swift to hear. One measures the heat at both ends; the other starts with the ears. Neither cancels the other.
Two old voices, saying slow down, each in its own words.

how: Jewish ethical teaching works on temperament as a practice; Avot 5:11's four tempers are studied with chapter five on summer Shabbat afternoons, and some students track their own anger as part of mussar, ethical self-work.

s: Avot says a good person never gets angry
it grades how fast anger comes and goes; the chasid is hard to anger and easy to calm.
the Letter of James also says slow to wrath
'swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath' (James 1:19, KJV).

games.q: your dad says he's slow to anger, so once he's angry he gets to stay mad for days. what would Avot point out?
o: slow to anger is half; Avot's chasid is also quick to calm down.
he's the best kind already; being slow to anger is all that counts.
staying angry is fine, as long as he never lets it show.
games.why: hard to anger and hard to calm is a mixed case in Avot: the gain is canceled by the loss. the chasid is slow in and quick out.

practice: Bring to mind a small irritation from this week, not the biggest one. Let it warm up for one breath, then count how many slow breaths it takes to cool, with each exhale longer than the inhale. Notice the number without judging it.

wordCard.voice: Slow to anger: in Avot, the chasid is hard to anger and easy to calm. Both speeds count.

orig.note: Hebrew: hard to anger, the first half of the chasid's temper in Avot 5:11.

carryVoice: For today: slow to anger, and quick to come back once the heat is gone. See you soon.
